question: A student defines an infectious disease as a condition caused by a pathogenic microorganism. Which of the following organism classes is included in that definition?
cited_learning_objective: Define "infectious disease" and the major classes of microorganisms that cause this medical condition.

options.text: Bacteria as a class of disease-causing organisms
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists bacteria among the major classes that cause infectious disease; the slides state "Bacteria" as a cause of infectious disease. If the lecture had excluded bacteria, this would be incorrect.

options.text: Nonbiological toxins unrelated to microbes
options.rationale: Wrong: Nonbiological toxins are not microorganisms; to be correct this option would need to be a microbial class such as viruses.

options.text: Psychogenic disorders without microbial involvement
options.rationale: Wrong: Psychogenic disorders are not caused by microbes; this would be correct only if the lecture redefined infectious disease to include noninfectious causes.

options.text: Mechanical injuries from trauma without infection
options.rationale: Wrong: Mechanical injuries are not microbial; would be correct only if the definition included noninfectious injury.

options.text: Nutritional deficiencies causing systemic disease
options.rationale: Wrong: Nutritional deficiencies are noninfectious; would be correct only if the lecture broadened the definition beyond microorganisms.

question: Which term best describes a microorganism that typically causes disease only when host defenses are impaired?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast Strict vs. opportunistic pathogens

options.text: Opportunistic pathogen as a conditional disease agent
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture defines opportunistic pathogens as those that cause disease in immunocompromised hosts or when barriers are disrupted; this matches the slide description.

options.text: Strict pathogen that always causes disease in hosts
options.rationale: Wrong: A strict pathogen is associated with disease regardless of host immune status; this would be correct only if the organism caused disease in healthy hosts.

options.text: Commensal organism that never causes disease
options.rationale: Wrong: Commensals can be part of normal microbiota and sometimes cause disease; would be correct only if they never invaded tissues.

options.text: Saprophytic organism living only on dead matter
options.rationale: Wrong: Saprophytes feed on dead organic matter and are not defined by causing disease in immunocompromised hosts; would be correct only if the lecture labeled them opportunistic.

options.text: Obligate pathogen that requires a host to survive
options.rationale: Wrong: Obligate pathogens always cause disease and often require a host; would be correct only if they were defined as conditional on host immunity.

question: A patient develops an infection from their own skin flora after a surgical incision. According to the lecture classifications, this infection is best described as which type?
cited_learning_objective: Define Exogenous vs. Endogenous infections

options.text: Endogenous infection originating from host microbiota
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture defines endogenous infections as invasion by agents already on or in the body (host microbiota), matching this scenario.

options.text: Exogenous infection acquired from an external source
options.rationale: Wrong: Exogenous infections come from outside the host; this would be correct only if the pathogen were introduced from the environment or another person.

options.text: Community-acquired infection from public exposure
options.rationale: Wrong: Community-acquired implies acquisition outside healthcare settings; would be correct only if the infection was contracted outside the surgical context.

options.text: Zoonotic infection transmitted from an animal source
options.rationale: Wrong: Zoonotic infections originate from animals; would be correct only if an animal source were implicated.

options.text: Vector-borne infection transmitted by an arthropod
options.rationale: Wrong: Vector-borne implies arthropod transmission; would be correct only if an insect bite introduced the pathogen.

question: Which phrase best matches the lecture definition of a nosocomial infection?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast Community acquired (CAI) vs. healthcare-associated (HAI) infections

options.text: Infection acquired during a hospital stay
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture states that nosocomial infections are acquired during a hospital stay; this directly matches the slide definition.

options.text: Infection acquired in the community before hospitalization
options.rationale: Wrong: Community-acquired infections occur outside healthcare facilities; would be correct only if the infection preceded hospital exposure.

options.text: Infection transmitted from animals to humans
options.rationale: Wrong: Zoonotic infections are animal-derived; would be correct only if an animal source caused the hospital infection.

options.text: Infection caused by a medical intervention outside hospital
options.rationale: Wrong: Iatrogenic infections result from medical interventions and can occur outside hospitals; would be correct only if the cause was a procedure rather than hospital stay.

options.text: Infection due to contaminated food consumed in hospital cafeteria
options.rationale: Wrong: While possible, this is a specific exogenous source; would be correct only if the cafeteria exposure was documented as the acquisition event.

question: Which of the following is an example of an emerging infectious disease as described in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Define emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases

options.text: A newly recognized disease appearing in humans
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture defines emerging infectious diseases as new diseases not previously seen in humans; this option captures that definition.

options.text: A long-known disease with stable incidence over decades
options.rationale: Wrong: That describes an endemic disease; would be correct only if incidence were increasing or newly appearing.

options.text: A disease eradicated worldwide with no cases
options.rationale: Wrong: Eradicated diseases are not emerging; would be correct only if new cases reappeared globally.

options.text: A chronic noninfectious metabolic disorder
options.rationale: Wrong: Noninfectious disorders are outside the lecture's infectious disease definition; would be correct only if reclassified as infectious.

options.text: A vaccine-preventable disease with declining incidence
options.rationale: Wrong: Declining incidence does not indicate emergence; would be correct only if incidence were increasing or newly appearing.

question: Which anatomical portal of entry is correctly paired with the transmission mode described in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the common anatomical portals of entry by infectious agents and modes of microbial transmission

options.text: Conjunctiva entry associated with aerosol exposure
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists the conjunctiva as a portal and includes aerosol/respiratory droplets under inhalation/direct contact modes, making this pairing accurate.

options.text: Placenta entry associated with fomite transmission
options.rationale: Wrong: Placental (vertical) transmission is mother-to-child, not via fomites; would be correct only if the pathogen crossed the placenta from contaminated surfaces.

options.text: Urethral entry associated with vector-borne transmission
options.rationale: Wrong: Urethral entry is linked to sexual contact or direct contact, not vector bites; would be correct only if an arthropod directly inoculated the urethra.

options.text: Broken skin entry associated with ingestion transmission
options.rationale: Wrong: Broken skin is typically direct contact or inoculation, not ingestion; would be correct only if contaminated food caused skin breach.

options.text: Eye entry associated with vertical mother to child transfer
options.rationale: Wrong: Eye (conjunctiva) exposure is not vertical transmission; would be correct only if maternal infection directly inoculated the neonate's conjunctiva during birth.

question: A virus transmitted by mosquitoes is best classified by which term used in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Define zoonotic infection and arboviruses

options.text: Arbovirus transmitted via an arthropod vector
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture defines arboviruses as viruses transmitted through vectors (arthropods) such as mosquitoes; this matches the slide content.

options.text: Endogenous virus originating from host microbiota
options.rationale: Wrong: Endogenous infections arise from the host's own microbiota; would be correct only if the virus were latent within the host flora.

options.text: Fomite-borne virus transmitted by inanimate objects
options.rationale: Wrong: Fomite transmission involves contaminated surfaces, not arthropod vectors; would be correct only if the virus spread via objects.

options.text: Obligate intracellular bacterium transmitted by ticks
options.rationale: Wrong: This mixes bacterial and viral categories; would be correct only if the pathogen were a tick-borne obligate intracellular bacterium like Rickettsia.

options.text: Direct-contact virus transmitted by sexual activity
options.rationale: Wrong: Sexual transmission is direct contact, not vector-borne; would be correct only if sexual contact were the route.

question: Which factor described in the lecture increases the likelihood that an exposure will overcome host defenses and cause infection?
cited_learning_objective: Define inoculum size, tissue tropism, and how both host and microbial factors can impact pathogenesis

options.text: A larger inoculum of invading organisms at exposure
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture states that larger numbers of invading organisms (inoculum) are more likely to overcome host defenses, directly supporting this option.

options.text: Narrow tissue tropism limiting pathogen attachment
options.rationale: Wrong: Narrow tropism restricts where a pathogen can infect; would be correct only if the tissue targeted were inaccessible to the pathogen.

options.text: Robust host immune competence without compromise
options.rationale: Wrong: Strong immunity reduces infection risk; would be correct only if the host were immunocompromised instead.

options.text: Low pathogen virulence factor expression during invasion
options.rationale: Wrong: Lower virulence reduces pathogenicity; would be correct only if virulence factors increased.

options.text: Entry via a route with high physical barriers intact
options.rationale: Wrong: Intact barriers decrease infection risk; would be correct only if barriers were breached.

question: Which statement best reflects the lecture's description of tissue tropism?
cited_learning_objective: Define inoculum size, tissue tropism, and how both host and microbial factors can impact pathogenesis

options.text: Tissue tropism is the host tissue a pathogen preferentially targets
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture defines tissue tropism as the host tissue where the pathogen likes to colonize or target, and notes factors like receptors and tissue properties.

options.text: Tissue tropism means a pathogen infects all tissues equally
options.rationale: Wrong: Tropism implies specificity, not uniform infection; would be correct only if the pathogen lacked specificity.

options.text: Tissue tropism refers to the pathogen's environmental reservoir
options.rationale: Wrong: Reservoirs are external sources; would be correct only if the lecture redefined tropism as reservoir preference.

options.text: Tissue tropism is solely determined by inoculum size
options.rationale: Wrong: Tropism depends on receptors and tissue properties, not just inoculum; would be correct only if inoculum were the only determinant.

options.text: Tissue tropism indicates the pathogen's resistance to disinfectants
options.rationale: Wrong: Resistance to disinfectants is unrelated to tissue targeting; would be correct only if the lecture linked tropism to environmental resistance.

question: Which replication strategy is characteristic of all viruses according to the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast intracellular versus extracellular replication of microbial pathogens, and identify how most viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites replicate within the host

options.text: Obligate intracellular replication inside host cells
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture states that all viruses require intracellular replication and are obligate intracellular pathogens.

options.text: Extracellular replication exclusively in tissue fluids
options.rationale: Wrong: Most viruses replicate inside cells, not extracellularly; would be correct only for pathogens that complete life cycles extracellularly.

options.text: Facultative extracellular replication in both niches
options.rationale: Wrong: Viruses are not facultative extracellular; would be correct only if viruses could reproduce outside cells.

options.text: Spore-forming extracellular replication like helminths
options.rationale: Wrong: Helminths often replicate extracellularly; would be correct only if viruses formed spores and replicated extracellularly.

options.text: Autonomous replication independent of host cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Viruses cannot replicate independently; would be correct only if they encoded all necessary replication machinery.

question: Which organism from the lecture is given as an example of a facultative intracellular bacterium?
cited_learning_objective: Explain what is meant by obligate intracellular growth compared with facultative intracellular growth

options.text: Listeria monocytogenes as a facultative intracellular bacterium
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists Listeria monocytogenes as an example of facultative intracellular growth, able to live inside and outside cells.

options.text: Chlamydia species as a facultative intracellular bacterium
options.rationale: Wrong: Chlamydia are obligate intracellular organisms; would be correct only if they could replicate extracellularly.

options.text: Rickettsia species as a facultative intracellular bacterium
options.rationale: Wrong: Rickettsia are obligate intracellular; would be correct only if they were facultative.

options.text: Most helminths as facultative intracellular bacteria
options.rationale: Wrong: Helminths are multicellular parasites and typically extracellular; would be correct only if they were bacteria with facultative intracellular growth.

options.text: All viruses as facultative intracellular organisms
options.rationale: Wrong: Viruses are obligate intracellular, not facultative; would be correct only if viruses could replicate outside cells.

question: A patient is colonized by a bacterium that is later cleared without disease. According to the lecture, this outcome is best termed which of the following?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the various outcomes of microbial entry: transient colonization, permanent colonization, and disease

options.text: Transient colonization cleared without causing disease
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture describes transient colonization as organisms quickly cleared with no disease, matching this scenario.

options.text: Permanent colonization establishing normal microbiota
options.rationale: Wrong: Permanent colonization implies long-term presence; would be correct only if the organism persisted.

options.text: Carrier state with ongoing asymptomatic shedding
options.rationale: Wrong: A carrier sheds organisms chronically; would be correct only if shedding persisted despite lack of symptoms.

options.text: Acute infectious disease causing host damage
options.rationale: Wrong: Disease implies host damage; would be correct only if symptoms and damage occurred.

options.text: Latent infection with periodic reactivation episodes
options.rationale: Wrong: Latency involves dormancy and reactivation; would be correct only if the organism entered a dormant state.

question: Which term from the lecture describes a host who transmits organisms but shows no symptoms?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the various outcomes of microbial entry: transient colonization, permanent colonization, and disease

options.text: Carrier state shedding organisms without symptoms
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture defines a carrier as a host who can transmit disease while not experiencing symptoms, matching this option.

options.text: Symptomatic patient actively showing disease signs
options.rationale: Wrong: Symptomatic patients show signs; would be correct only if symptoms were present.

options.text: Transient colonized individual immediately cleared
options.rationale: Wrong: Transient colonization is cleared quickly and typically does not involve prolonged shedding; would be correct only if shedding were absent.

options.text: Permanent colonized individual never shedding organisms
options.rationale: Wrong: Permanent colonization can include shedding; would be correct only if the organism never exited the host.

options.text: Latent carrier with continuous symptomatic infection
options.rationale: Wrong: Latent carriers are asymptomatic during latency; would be correct only if symptoms were continuous.

question: Which statement best captures the lecture's point about the relationship between transmissibility and virulence?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how pathogens spread to new hosts

options.text: Transmissibility and virulence are independent traits
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture explicitly notes that transmissibility and virulence are not linked traits, indicating independence.

options.text: Higher virulence always increases transmissibility
options.rationale: Wrong: The lecture states they are not linked; would be correct only if virulence directly determined transmissibility.

options.text: Lower transmissibility always reduces virulence
options.rationale: Wrong: No direct inverse relationship is asserted; would be correct only if a causal link existed.

options.text: Transmissibility equals virulence in all pathogens
options.rationale: Wrong: The lecture contradicts this; would be correct only if the two were synonymous.

options.text: Virulence solely determines carrier state duration
options.rationale: Wrong: Carrier duration depends on host and pathogen factors, not just virulence; would be correct only if virulence were the only determinant.

question: Using the lecture's definition, what does the basic reproduction number R0 represent?
cited_learning_objective: Define Carrier, Shedding, Asymptomatic shedding, Reproduction number, Effective reproduction number, Herd immunity

options.text: Average new infections from one case in a fully susceptible population
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture defines R0 as the average number of new infections produced by a single infected individual in a fully susceptible population.

options.text: Average new infections accounting for immunity at a given time
options.rationale: Wrong: That describes the effective reproduction number (Rt), not R0; would be correct only if immunity were absent.

options.text: Proportion of population immune required for herd protection
options.rationale: Wrong: That is the herd immunity threshold derived from R0; would be correct only if phrased as threshold rather than R0 itself.

options.text: Duration of infectiousness in days for a single case
options.rationale: Wrong: Duration of infectiousness is a factor influencing R0 but is not R0 itself; would be correct only if R0 were defined as time-based.

options.text: Contact rate between immune individuals only
options.rationale: Wrong: R0 concerns susceptible individuals, not immune-only contacts; would be correct only if the population were fully immune.

question: A public health team wants to estimate how many people must be immunized to achieve herd immunity. Which lecture concept directly informs that calculation?
cited_learning_objective: Define Carrier, Shedding, Asymptomatic shedding, Reproduction number, Effective reproduction number, Herd immunity

options.text: The basic reproduction number R0 determines herd immunity threshold
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture links R0 to predictions about what proportion of the population needs immunization to prevent spread and achieve herd immunity.

options.text: The incubation period alone determines herd immunity
options.rationale: Wrong: Incubation period affects dynamics but not directly the herd immunity threshold; would be correct only if incubation determined transmission potential.

options.text: The pathogen's tissue tropism determines immunization proportion
options.rationale: Wrong: Tropism affects disease manifestations but not the herd immunity calculation; would be correct only if tropism altered R0.

options.text: The method of sterilization used in hospitals determines herd immunity
options.rationale: Wrong: Sterilization reduces transmission in healthcare settings but does not set population-level immunity thresholds; would be correct only if sterilization achieved population immunity.

options.text: The presence of fomites alone determines herd immunity
options.rationale: Wrong: Fomites are a transmission route but do not define herd immunity; would be correct only if fomite transmission dominated and altered R0.

question: Which control measure listed in the lecture directly reduces contact rate to lower transmission?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the various outcomes of microbial entry: transient colonization, permanent colonization, and disease

options.text: Physical distancing to reduce contact between individuals
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists physical distancing (and masks, PPE) as measures that reduce contact rate and thus transmission.

options.text: Autoclaving surgical instruments to sterilize equipment
options.rationale: Wrong: Autoclaving sterilizes instruments but does not directly reduce person-to-person contact; would be correct only if instrument-mediated contact were the main route.

options.text: Chlorination of water to modify proteins of microbes
options.rationale: Wrong: Chlorination disinfects water but is not a contact-reduction measure; would be correct only if waterborne contact were the primary transmission.

options.text: UV irradiation of surfaces to denature proteins
options.rationale: Wrong: UV disinfects surfaces but does not reduce interpersonal contact; would be correct only if surface contact were the dominant route.

options.text: Filtration of air to remove larger particles
options.rationale: Wrong: Filtration reduces airborne particles but is not a behavioral contact reduction; would be correct only if airborne particles were the main transmission and filtration reduced exposures.

question: Which pair correctly contrasts sterilization and disinfection as defined in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Define and differentiate the following terms: sterilization, disinfection; septic, aseptic, antiseptic; bactericidal, bacteriostatic, germicide-the use of -static vs. -cidal; disinfectant vs. antiseptic

options.text: Sterilization destroys all microorganisms; disinfection reduces organisms to safe levels
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture defines sterilization as destruction of all microorganisms and disinfection as reducing organisms to levels unlikely to cause disease.

options.text: Disinfection destroys all microorganisms; sterilization reduces organisms to safe levels
options.rationale: Wrong: This reverses the definitions; would be correct only if the lecture had swapped the terms.

options.text: Sterilization refers only to antiseptic use on skin
options.rationale: Wrong: Sterilization is for complete elimination, often of instruments, not limited to skin antisepsis; would be correct only if the lecture redefined sterilization.

options.text: Disinfection always eliminates bacterial spores completely
options.rationale: Wrong: Disinfection does not reliably inactivate spores; would be correct only if the disinfectant used was sporicidal and applied under sterilizing conditions.

options.text: Sterilization is synonymous with antisepsis on living tissue
options.rationale: Wrong: Antisepsis is for living tissue and may not sterilize; would be correct only if antiseptics achieved complete sterilization on tissue.

question: An agent that inhibits bacterial growth without killing cells is best termed which label from the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Define and differentiate the following terms: bactericidal, bacteriostatic, germicide-the use of -static vs. -cidal

options.text: Bacteriostatic agent that inhibits bacterial growth
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture explains '-static' agents inhibit growth (bacteriostatic) while '-cidal' agents kill microbes.

options.text: Bactericidal agent that kills bacteria outright
options.rationale: Wrong: Bactericidal agents kill bacteria; would be correct only if the agent caused cell death rather than growth inhibition.

options.text: Germicide that only inhibits viral replication
options.rationale: Wrong: Germicide generally inactivates microbes; would be correct only if defined narrowly for viruses in the lecture.

options.text: Antiseptic that sterilizes surgical instruments
options.rationale: Wrong: Antiseptics are for living tissue and do not necessarily sterilize instruments; would be correct only if antiseptics achieved sterilization.

options.text: Disinfectant that promotes bacterial growth on surfaces
options.rationale: Wrong: Disinfectants reduce microbial load, not promote growth; would be correct only if the product were contaminated and supported growth.

question: Which chemical agent category from the lecture primarily disrupts cell membranes?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the general mechanisms of action of common chemical and physical agents for sterilization, disinfections, and antisepsis

options.text: Alcohols and detergents disrupt microbial cell membranes
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists alcohol (70% ethanol) and detergents as agents that disrupt cell membranes.

options.text: Chlorine compounds primarily act by disrupting membranes
options.rationale: Wrong: Chlorine mainly modifies proteins and DNA; would be correct only if chlorine's primary action were membrane disruption.

options.text: Heavy metals act mainly by forming thymine dimers
options.rationale: Wrong: Heavy metals modify proteins; thymine dimer formation is caused by UV radiation, not metals.

options.text: Crystal violet primarily modifies nucleic acids
options.rationale: Wrong: Crystal violet affects cell walls and is used as a stain; would be correct only if it were described as a DNA modifier.

options.text: Hydrogen peroxide acts exclusively by detergent-like action
options.rationale: Wrong: Hydrogen peroxide modifies proteins and generates radicals; would be correct only if its mechanism were detergent-like.

question: Which physical sterilization method from the lecture is capable of inactivating bacterial spores when applied correctly?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the general mechanisms of action of common chemical and physical agents for sterilization, disinfections, and antisepsis

options.text: Autoclaving with moist heat at 121°C under pressure
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture describes autoclaving (121°C, 15 psi, 15-20 min) as inactivating bacterial spores, making it the standard sterilization method.

options.text: Pasteurization at 63°C for 30 minutes to sterilize
options.rationale: Wrong: Pasteurization does not sterilize and does not inactivate spores; would be correct only if pasteurization parameters were changed to sterilizing conditions.

options.text: Dry heat at low temperature for short time periods
options.rationale: Wrong: Dry heat requires higher temperatures and longer times to sterilize; would be correct only if parameters matched sterilizing conditions.

options.text: UV irradiation penetrating deep into packaged products
options.rationale: Wrong: UV is surface-limited and does not reliably inactivate spores in complex items; would be correct only if penetration were sufficient.

options.text: Filtration through 0.22 μm pores removing viruses
options.rationale: Wrong: 0.22 μm filtration removes bacteria but not most viruses; would be correct only if pore size were small enough to exclude viruses.

question: Which radiation type described in the lecture is most suitable for sterilizing packaged, sealed products due to deep penetration?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the general mechanisms of action of common chemical and physical agents for sterilization, disinfections, and antisepsis

options.text: Gamma irradiation using radioisotopes for deep penetration
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture notes gamma irradiation penetrates beyond surfaces and is used for sterilizing complex or packaged items.

options.text: Ultraviolet light for deep sterilization of sealed packages
options.rationale: Wrong: UV is surface-limited and cannot penetrate sealed packaging; would be correct only if UV could penetrate packaging.

options.text: Electron beam with no depth penetration for sealed goods
options.rationale: Wrong: E-beam has limited penetration compared to gamma rays; would be correct only if depth were not required.

options.text: Microwave radiation causing thymine dimer formation
options.rationale: Wrong: Microwaves heat and are not primarily used for sterilization via thymine dimers; thymine dimers are caused by UV.

options.text: Visible light irradiation producing reactive oxygen species
options.rationale: Wrong: Visible light is not used for sterilization; would be correct only if it generated sufficient reactive species to sterilize.

question: Which filtration pore size from the lecture would reliably remove most bacteria but not viruses?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the general mechanisms of action of common chemical and physical agents for sterilization, disinfections, and antisepsis

options.text: 0.22 micrometer pore size filters remove most bacteria
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture indicates 0.22 μm filtration removes bacteria and spores but not viruses, which are smaller.

options.text: 10 micrometer filters designed to exclude viruses
options.rationale: Wrong: 10 μm is far too large to exclude viruses or bacteria; would be correct only if pore size were much smaller.

options.text: 100 nanometer filters that exclude human cells only
options.rationale: Wrong: 100 nm (~0.1 μm) can exclude many viruses but not human cells; would be correct only if the filter targeted cells specifically.

options.text: 1 millimeter mesh used for viral sterilization
options.rationale: Wrong: 1 mm is orders of magnitude too large; would be correct only if the mesh were microscopic.

options.text: 0.001 micrometer filters that remove DNA molecules
options.rationale: Wrong: Such pore sizes are impractical and not described in the lecture; would be correct only if ultrafiltration at that scale were used.

question: A hospital plans to disinfect a surface contaminated with an enveloped virus. According to the lecture, which class of chemical agent would be expected to disrupt the viral envelope effectively?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the general mechanisms of action of common chemical and physical agents for sterilization, disinfections, and antisepsis

options.text: Alcohol-based disinfectant that disrupts lipid membranes
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists alcohols (70% ethanol) as agents that disrupt cell membranes and envelopes, making them effective against enveloped viruses.

options.text: Iodine solution that acts solely by filtration
options.rationale: Wrong: Iodine modifies proteins and is not a filtration method; would be correct only if iodine were described as a physical filter.

options.text: 0.22 μm membrane filtration to inactivate enveloped viruses
options.rationale: Wrong: Filtration removes particles but 0.22 μm may not remove all viruses; would be correct only if pore size excluded the virus.

options.text: Dry heat at low temperature for short time to denature envelope
options.rationale: Wrong: Dry heat requires high temperature and long time to inactivate pathogens; would be correct only if parameters matched sterilization conditions.

options.text: Crystal violet application to cleave viral nucleic acids
options.rationale: Wrong: Crystal violet is a stain and not primarily a nucleic acid-cleaving disinfectant; would be correct only if it were shown to inactivate viruses via DNA cleavage.

question: A researcher measures the effective reproduction number Rt during an outbreak after a vaccination campaign. Which lecture concept explains why Rt differs from R0 in this context?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the significance of & how to interpret reproduction number compared to effective reproduction number

options.text: Rt accounts for existing immunity and control measures reducing spread
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture explains Rt (effective reproduction number) reflects real-world conditions including immunity from prior infection or vaccination and public health measures.

options.text: Rt assumes a fully susceptible population like R0 does
options.rationale: Wrong: Rt differs from R0 by accounting for immunity; would be correct only if immunity were absent.

options.text: Rt measures only pathogen virulence independent of behavior
options.rationale: Wrong: Rt depends on transmissibility, contact rate, and behavior; would be correct only if behavior were constant and irrelevant.

options.text: Rt is the theoretical maximum contagiousness without interventions
options.rationale: Wrong: That describes R0, not Rt; would be correct only if interventions were absent.

options.text: Rt equals the incubation period multiplied by contact rate
options.rationale: Wrong: Rt is not a simple product of incubation and contact rate; would be correct only if the lecture defined it that way.

question: A clinician must choose between sterilization and disinfection for an instrument contacting sterile body cavities. Based on the lecture, which is the appropriate requirement?
cited_learning_objective: Define and differentiate the following terms: sterilization, disinfection; septic, aseptic, antiseptic; bactericidal, bacteriostatic, germicide-the use of -static vs. -cidal; disinfectant vs. antiseptic

options.text: Sterilization to destroy all microorganisms before use
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture emphasizes sterilization is required for surgical procedures and equipment contacting sterile body sites because it destroys all microorganisms including spores.

options.text: Disinfection to reduce organisms to safe levels for sterile cavities
options.rationale: Wrong: Disinfection reduces microbial load but does not guarantee sterility; would be correct only if the instrument did not enter sterile cavities.

options.text: Antisepsis on the instrument surface before insertion
options.rationale: Wrong: Antiseptics are for living tissue and are not substitutes for instrument sterilization; would be correct only if the instrument contacted only intact skin.

options.text: Pasteurization of the instrument to kill bacterial spores
options.rationale: Wrong: Pasteurization does not inactivate spores and is unsuitable for instruments; would be correct only if pasteurization parameters achieved sterilization.

options.text: UV surface disinfection as equivalent to autoclaving
options.rationale: Wrong: UV is surface-limited and not equivalent to autoclaving for sterilization; would be correct only if UV penetration and dose matched sterilization requirements.

question: A patient with HIV has recurrent infections from organisms normally present on skin. Using lecture concepts, which pathogen classification best explains this pattern?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast Strict vs. opportunistic pathogens

options.text: Opportunistic pathogens causing disease in immunocompromised host
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture describes opportunistic pathogens as those that typically do not cause disease in immunocompetent hosts but do in immunocompromised individuals, matching this clinical pattern.

options.text: Strict pathogens that always cause disease regardless of immunity
options.rationale: Wrong: Strict pathogens cause disease even in healthy hosts; would be correct only if infections occurred in immunocompetent individuals.

options.text: Zoonotic pathogens acquired from animal exposure
options.rationale: Wrong: Zoonoses originate from animals; would be correct only if animal contact were the source.

options.text: Vector-borne pathogens transmitted by arthropods
options.rationale: Wrong: Vector-borne implies arthropod transmission; would be correct only if insect bites introduced the organisms.

options.text: Environmental saprophytes that never colonize humans
options.rationale: Wrong: Saprophytes feed on dead matter and may not colonize humans; would be correct only if the organisms were noncolonizing environmental species.

question: A lab finds a bacterium that can replicate both inside macrophages and in extracellular fluid. According to the lecture, how should this organism be classified regarding intracellular growth?
cited_learning_objective: Explain what is meant by obligate intracellular growth compared with facultative intracellular growth

options.text: Facultative intracellular organism able to grow inside and outside cells
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture defines facultative intracellular organisms as those that can live and reproduce both inside and outside host cells, matching this description.

options.text: Obligate intracellular organism requiring host cells to replicate
options.rationale: Wrong: Obligate intracellular organisms can only replicate inside cells; would be correct only if extracellular replication were impossible.

options.text: Extracellular organism that never invades host cells
options.rationale: Wrong: The organism in the stem invades cells; would be correct only if intracellular replication were absent.

options.text: Prion-like agent replicating without nucleic acids
options.rationale: Wrong: Prions are proteinaceous infectious particles and do not replicate intracellularly like bacteria; would be correct only if the agent lacked nucleic acids.

options.text: Vector-borne obligate parasite transmitted by insects
options.rationale: Wrong: Vector-borne status is about transmission, not intracellular capability; would be correct only if the organism required a vector and intracellular growth exclusively.

question: A patient sheds virus particles before symptom onset. Based on the lecture, which term best describes this phenomenon?
cited_learning_objective: Define Carrier, Shedding, Asymptomatic shedding, Reproduction number, Effective reproduction number, Herd immunity

options.text: Asymptomatic shedding of infectious agents before symptoms
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture explains that shedding can begin before symptoms (asymptomatic shedding), allowing transmission prior to clinical disease.

options.text: Permanent colonization without any shedding
options.rationale: Wrong: Permanent colonization may include shedding; would be correct only if no organisms exited the host.

options.text: Transient colonization that always causes immediate symptoms
options.rationale: Wrong: Transient colonization is often cleared and may not cause symptoms; would be correct only if symptoms always followed colonization.

options.text: Iatrogenic infection resulting from medical intervention
options.rationale: Wrong: Iatrogenic refers to infections caused by medical procedures, not pre-symptomatic shedding; would be correct only if a procedure caused the shedding.

options.text: Zoonotic transmission from an animal reservoir
options.rationale: Wrong: Zoonotic refers to animal-to-human transmission, not asymptomatic human shedding; would be correct only if an animal source were involved.

question: A public health official observes Rt falling below 1 after interventions. According to the lecture, what does this indicate about the epidemic?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the significance of & how to interpret reproduction number compared to effective reproduction number

options.text: The epidemic is declining because each case infects fewer than one person
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture states that Rt   1; would be correct only if Rt exceeded one.

options.text: Herd immunity has been achieved regardless of immunity levels
options.rationale: Wrong: Rt < 1 can result from interventions or immunity; herd immunity is not automatically achieved solely because Rt < 1.

options.text: R0 has increased above the effective reproduction number
options.rationale: Wrong: R0 is theoretical maximum in a susceptible population; this statement is not the direct implication of Rt < 1.

options.text: The pathogen's virulence has necessarily decreased
options.rationale: Wrong: A decrease in Rt reflects transmission dynamics, not necessarily virulence changes; would be correct only if virulence reduction caused fewer transmissions.

question: A clinician must choose an antiseptic for skin prior to incision. Based on the lecture distinctions, which statement is true about antiseptics versus disinfectants?
cited_learning_objective: Define and differentiate the following terms: sterilization, disinfection; septic, aseptic, antiseptic; bactericidal, bacteriostatic, germicide-the use of -static vs. -cidal; disinfectant vs. antiseptic

options.text: Antiseptics are used on living tissue; disinfectants on inanimate surfaces
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture differentiates antiseptics (used on living tissue) from disinfectants (used on surfaces and objects).

options.text: Disinfectants are safe for application to mucous membranes
options.rationale: Wrong: Disinfectants are generally not for living tissue; would be correct only if a disinfectant were specifically labeled as safe for mucous membranes.

options.text: Antiseptics always achieve complete sterilization of instruments
options.rationale: Wrong: Antiseptics reduce microbial load on tissue but do not sterilize instruments; would be correct only if antiseptics were proven to sterilize instruments.

options.text: Antiseptics function primarily by filtration of microbes
options.rationale: Wrong: Antiseptics act chemically, not by filtration; would be correct only if a chemical acted as a physical filter.

options.text: Disinfectants are synonymous with bacteriostatic agents on skin
options.rationale: Wrong: Disinfectants are used on surfaces and may be bactericidal or bacteriostatic; would be correct only if disinfectants were defined as bacteriostatic on skin.

question: A researcher models an outbreak and finds R0 = 18 for a pathogen. Using the lecture examples, which disease is most comparable in contagiousness?
cited_learning_objective: Define Carrier, Shedding, Asymptomatic shedding, Reproduction number, Effective reproduction number, Herd immunity

options.text: Measles with very high basic reproduction number
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists measles with an R0 around 18 as an example of very high contagiousness, making it the comparable disease.

options.text: Ebola with low basic reproduction number near two
options.rationale: Wrong: Ebola has a much lower R0 (~2); would be correct only if the modeled pathogen had similar low transmissibility.

options.text: Hepatitis C with moderate reproduction number near two
options.rationale: Wrong: Hepatitis C is less contagious than measles; would be correct only if R0 were near two.

options.text: Mumps with reproduction number near ten
options.rationale: Wrong: Mumps has an R0 around 10, lower than 18; would be correct only if the modeled pathogen matched mumps' transmissibility.

options.text: HIV with reproduction number around four
options.rationale: Wrong: HIV's R0 is lower (~4) and transmission dynamics differ; would be correct only if the pathogen's R0 matched HIV.

question: A patient acquires an infection after a blood transfusion. According to the lecture categories, this is best described as which type of transmission?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the common anatomical portals of entry by infectious agents and modes of microbial transmission: inhalation, ingestion, direct contact, sexual contact, exchange of bodily fluids/tissues, vertical transmission, fomite, and vector-borne

options.text: Transmission via exchange of bodily fluids or tissues
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists exchange of bodily fluids/tissues (including blood products) as a transmission mode, matching transfusion-associated infection.

options.text: Vector-borne transmission via arthropod bite
options.rationale: Wrong: Vector-borne implies insect or arthropod transmission; would be correct only if an arthropod transmitted the pathogen.

options.text: Ingestion of contaminated food or water
options.rationale: Wrong: Ingestion is oral intake of contaminated substances; would be correct only if the transfusion involved contaminated oral intake.

options.text: Fomite transmission from inanimate surfaces
options.rationale: Wrong: Fomites are objects and surfaces; would be correct only if the transfusion equipment surface contamination caused infection.

options.text: Vertical transmission from mother to child during birth
options.rationale: Wrong: Vertical transmission is mother-to-child; would be correct only if the infection occurred during childbirth.

question: A clinician is deciding whether to use ethylene oxide gas or autoclaving for heat-sensitive surgical instruments. Based on the lecture, which statement is accurate about ethylene oxide?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the general mechanisms of action of common chemical and physical agents for sterilization, disinfections, and antisepsis

options.text: Ethylene oxide gas chemically modifies proteins and sterilizes heat-sensitive items
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists ethylene oxide gas among chemical sterilants that modify proteins and are used for heat-sensitive equipment.

options.text: Ethylene oxide is equivalent to pasteurization for sterilization
options.rationale: Wrong: Pasteurization does not sterilize; would be correct only if pasteurization achieved complete sterilization.

options.text: Ethylene oxide acts primarily by filtration through membranes
options.rationale: Wrong: Ethylene oxide is a chemical agent that modifies proteins, not a filtration method; would be correct only if it physically filtered microbes.

options.text: Ethylene oxide is ineffective against bacterial spores
options.rationale: Wrong: Ethylene oxide is used to sterilize and can inactivate spores; would be correct only if it lacked sporicidal activity.

options.text: Ethylene oxide sterilizes by generating thymine dimers in DNA
options.rationale: Wrong: Thymine dimers are caused by UV radiation; ethylene oxide modifies proteins and DNA differently.

question: A patient develops an infection after receiving contaminated donor tissue. Which lecture term best classifies this infection?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the common anatomical portals of entry by infectious agents and modes of microbial transmission: inhalation, ingestion, direct contact, sexual contact, exchange of bodily fluids/tissues, vertical transmission, fomite, and vector-borne

options.text: Transmission via exchange of bodily fluids or tissues during transplantation
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture includes exchange of bodily fluids/tissues and organ/tissue transplantation as transmission routes, matching contaminated donor tissue infection.

options.text: Vector-borne transmission by arthropod at time of transplant
options.rationale: Wrong: Vector-borne implies arthropod involvement; would be correct only if an arthropod transmitted the pathogen to the donor or recipient.

options.text: Ingestion of contaminated food during the transplant procedure
options.rationale: Wrong: Ingestion is oral intake; would be correct only if contaminated food caused the infection.

options.text: Vertical transmission from donor to recipient across placenta
options.rationale: Wrong: Vertical transmission is mother-to-child; would be correct only if the recipient were a fetus receiving tissue via placenta.

options.text: Fomite transmission from surgical instruments unrelated to tissue
options.rationale: Wrong: While fomites can transmit infection, the stem specifies contaminated donor tissue as the source; would be correct only if instruments were the contaminated source.

question: A pathogen that completes its life cycle entirely outside host cells is described in the lecture as which replication type?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast intracellular versus extracellular replication of microbial pathogens, and identify how most viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites replicate within the host

options.text: Extracellular replication occurring in tissues outside cells
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture defines extracellular replication as completion of the life cycle outside host cells, typical for most bacteria and helminths.

options.text: Obligate intracellular replication requiring host cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Obligate intracellular organisms require host cells; would be correct only if the pathogen could not replicate extracellularly.

options.text: Facultative intracellular replication only inside cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Facultative intracellular organisms can replicate both inside and outside cells; would be correct only if replication were exclusively intracellular.

options.text: Latent intracellular persistence without replication
options.rationale: Wrong: Latency involves dormancy; would be correct only if the organism did not complete a life cycle extracellularly.

options.text: Prion-mediated extracellular protein propagation
options.rationale: Wrong: Prions propagate by protein misfolding and are not typical extracellular life-cycle pathogens as described; would be correct only if prion propagation matched the lecture's extracellular definition.

question: A hospital implements hand hygiene, isolation, and contact tracing during an outbreak. According to the lecture, which of these directly reduces the duration of infectivity and thus Rt?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the various outcomes of microbial entry: transient colonization, permanent colonization, and disease

options.text: Identifying and treating symptomatic cases to shorten infectious period
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists identifying and treating symptomatic cases as a control measure that reduces duration of infectivity, thereby lowering Rt.

options.text: Isolation and quarantines that increase duration of infectivity
options.rationale: Wrong: Isolation reduces contact but does not increase infectious duration; would be correct only if isolation paradoxically prolonged infectiousness.

options.text: Hand hygiene that extends pathogen shedding time
options.rationale: Wrong: Hand hygiene reduces transmission and does not extend shedding; would be correct only if hygiene practices worsened infection control.

options.text: Contact tracing that eliminates the need for treatment
options.rationale: Wrong: Contact tracing identifies exposures but does not replace treatment; would be correct only if tracing directly cured infections.

options.text: Travel restrictions that increase individual infectiousness
options.rationale: Wrong: Travel restrictions reduce spread but do not increase infectiousness; would be correct only if restrictions somehow prolonged infection.

question: A surface disinfectant label claims 'virucidal, bactericidal, fungicidal, tuberculocidal.' Based on the lecture distinctions, which claim indicates the broadest spectrum of activity?
cited_learning_objective: Define and differentiate the following terms: sterilization, disinfection; septic, aseptic, antiseptic; bactericidal, bacteriostatic, germicide-the use of -static vs. -cidal; disinfectant vs. antiseptic

options.text: Virucidal, bactericidal, fungicidal, and tuberculocidal indicates broad activity
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture shows that '-cidal' indicates killing activity; listing multiple -cidal activities denotes a broad spectrum against viruses, bacteria, fungi, and mycobacteria.

options.text: Bacteriostatic label indicates broader activity than -cidal claims
options.rationale: Wrong: Bacteriostatic inhibits growth and is not broader than multiple -cidal claims; would be correct only if bacteriostatic covered all organism types.

options.text: Antiseptic labeling implies broader environmental sterilization
options.rationale: Wrong: Antiseptics are for living tissue and may not sterilize environments; would be correct only if antiseptics were proven to sterilize surfaces.

options.text: Disinfectant without -cidal claims is broader than -cidal labeled products
options.rationale: Wrong: Disinfectant without specific -cidal claims is less informative; would be correct only if unspecified disinfectants were proven broader.

options.text: Tuberculocidal alone indicates the broadest antimicrobial spectrum
options.rationale: Wrong: Tuberculocidal targets mycobacteria specifically and does not imply activity against all microbes; would be correct only if tuberculocidal agents were shown to kill all organism classes.

question: A clinician must choose between using 70% ethanol and a heavy-metal antiseptic for skin prep. Based on the lecture mechanisms, which statement is true about their primary actions?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the general mechanisms of action of common chemical and physical agents for sterilization, disinfections, and antisepsis

options.text: Ethanol disrupts membranes; heavy metals modify proteins
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists alcohols (70% ethanol) as disrupting cell membranes and heavy metals as modifying proteins, making this the accurate mechanistic pairing.

options.text: Ethanol modifies DNA; heavy metals act by filtration
options.rationale: Wrong: Ethanol primarily disrupts membranes, not DNA; heavy metals are chemical modifiers, not filters; would be correct only if mechanisms were misattributed.

options.text: Both ethanol and heavy metals act solely by creating thymine dimers
options.rationale: Wrong: Thymine dimers result from UV radiation, not chemical agents like ethanol or metals; would be correct only if UV were the mechanism.

options.text: Heavy metals disrupt membranes while ethanol crosslinks proteins
options.rationale: Wrong: This reverses the lecture mechanisms; would be correct only if the lecture described opposite actions.

options.text: Ethanol sterilizes spores while heavy metals only disinfect surfaces
options.rationale: Wrong: Ethanol does not reliably inactivate spores; would be correct only if ethanol were sporicidal under the conditions used.

question: A patient with a respiratory virus sheds high viral loads via aerosols. According to the lecture, which portal of entry in a new host is most directly implicated?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the common anatomical portals of entry by infectious agents and modes of microbial transmission: inhalation, ingestion, direct contact, sexual contact, exchange of bodily fluids/tissues, vertical transmission, fomite, and vector-borne

options.text: Nasal mucosa via inhalation of aerosolized particles
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists inhalation and respiratory droplets/aerosols as modes of transmission with the nose and respiratory mucosa as portals of entry.

options.text: Placental transfer to fetus during pregnancy
options.rationale: Wrong: Placental (vertical) transmission is mother-to-child and not the primary route for aerosol respiratory viruses; would be correct only if vertical transmission were documented.

options.text: Ingestion through contaminated food causing respiratory infection
options.rationale: Wrong: Ingestion leads to gastrointestinal exposure, not primary respiratory mucosal entry; would be correct only if the virus infected via the gut.

options.text: Vector-borne inoculation by arthropod bite into skin
options.rationale: Wrong: Vector-borne transmission involves arthropods and skin inoculation; would be correct only if an arthropod transmitted the virus.

options.text: Fomite contact with inanimate surfaces causing systemic infection
options.rationale: Wrong: Fomites can transfer virus to mucosa but are indirect; would be correct only if surface contact led to mucosal inoculation.
